articles.title: Majority of Americans, Canadians agree Trump’s tariffs were wrong: Poll
articles.summary: A majority of U.S. and Canadian adults in a new survey released Wednesday said they disagreed with President Trump’s decision to hike tariffs on goods imported by Canada. The Politico/Public First poll found that 83 percent of Canadians and 56 percent of Americans believe the increased import taxes on the U.S.’s northern neighbor were “wrong.”…
articles.body:
A majority of U.S. and Canadian adults in a new survey released Wednesday said they disagreed with President Trump’s decision to hike tariffs on goods imported by Canada.

The Politico/Public First poll found that 83 percent of Canadians and 56 percent of Americans believe the increased import taxes on the U.S.’s northern neighbor were “wrong.”

Another 26 percent of surveyed U.S. adults supported the Trump administration’s tariffs on Ottawa, while only 8 percent of Canadian respondents said the same.

The two groups were more split on the issue of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. Carney’s government levied duties as high as 50 percent on $27.6 billion in American imports, and they went into effect earlier this month.

Canada’s economic policies countered the Trump administration’s 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion in products imported into the U.S. Trump responded by threatening to impose 50 percent tariffs on imported trucks, cars, auto parts and steel going into effect on New Year’s Day.

Just more than 70 percent of Canadians in the latest poll said they approved of the prime minister’s actions. Another 33 percent of Americans agreed, while 31 percent said Carney’s levies were “wrong” and 35 percent were unsure.

Trump’s approval ratings have taken a dip amid the rising cost of living, which is tied to global energy shortages during the Iran war. The average price of standard and diesel gas has skyrocketed since the conflict began more than six months ago.

The president brushed aside these rising costs, saying recently at a political rally in North Carolina that hiked gas prices were a “very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done.”

In an NBC News poll released this week, 55 percent of the surveyed U.S. adults said the president’s policies have weakened the country’s economy. Additionally, a Marquette Law School survey conducted in July found 75 percent of American respondents said they do not believe the conflict was “worth the cost.”

The Politico poll was conducted among 2,064 U.S. adults and 2,199 Canadian adults from Sept. 13-15. The margin of error is approximately 2.2 percentage points for Americans and 2.1 for Canadians.

articles.title: Azerbaijan frees jailed Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
articles.summary: Martin Ryan is pardoned months after he was jailed on charges of spying, but a second Frenchman remains in prison.
articles.body:
French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying.

His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov.

Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev.

However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe.

It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list.

Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns.

Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years.

Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine".

The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans".

Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men.

Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative".

French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations.

Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon.

Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government.

Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China.

"I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court.

Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev.

articles.title: Can Ethiopia’s seven-group rebel alliance challenge Abiy Ahmed?
articles.summary: The alliance brings together movements with different enemies, claims and histories as tensions with Abiy rise.
articles.body:
Two days after seven Ethiopian armed groups announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival and pledged to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, a senior official of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) was asked whether the statement amounted to a declaration of war.

He hesitated, then answered with a question of his own.

He was speaking to Kjetil Tronvoll, professor of peace and conflict studies at Oslo New University College, who told Al Jazeera that the answer captured what the new rebel alliance had changed.

It has not created a single, coherent military force capable of marching on Addis Ababa. It has brought several of Ethiopia’s separate conflicts into the same political framework and, potentially, into the same military calculation.

The question now is how much further that can spread and whether seven movements with different enemies, territorial claims and histories can actually fight as one.

On Tuesday, drones struck two schools in Alamata, in southern Tigray, and the town’s mayor said 14 civilians were killed and 22 wounded. The account could not be independently verified, and the federal government did not immediately comment.

By Wednesday, Tigrayan forces had seized Alula Aba Nega International Airport in Mekelle, AFP reported, citing an airport employee and a Western embassy security source. The airport employee said staff had been told there were no flights.

The alliance, whose founding statement Fano commander Zemene Kassie read on Tigrai TV on Sunday, brings together the Amhara Fano National Movement, the TPLF and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), along with the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front, the Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement.

It promises a transitional administration once Abiy is gone.

Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, told Reuters that the members had been collaborating for some time with Eritrean financial backing, an accusation Asmara has repeatedly denied.

The TPLF dominated Ethiopia for 27 years, until Abiy took power in 2018 and pushed it to the margins.

In November 2020, the federal army, backed by Eritrean troops and Amhara forces, went to war with it. The conflict became one of the deadliest in Ethiopia’s modern history. African Union mediator Olusegun Obasanjo believes that about 600,000 people died, though estimates of the toll have varied.

That war ended in November 2022 with an agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa.

It was a permanent cessation of hostilities. It silenced the guns and set terms for Tigray’s disarmament, but left critical questions for later, above all Western Tigray, the fertile territory claimed by both sides and administered by Amhara forces since the war.

Only Addis Ababa and the TPLF signed. Neither Eritrea nor the Amhara forces had a seat.

Jawar Mohammed, the Oromo politician who was once an ally of Abiy and later spent time in prison, told Al Jazeera that shutting them out gave them every reason to wreck the deal.

The new alliance brings together forces that were excluded from the Pretoria negotiations with one of the agreement’s signatories.

The quiet it created ended in May, when the TPLF restored the legislative council that existed before the war and installed its chairman, Debretsion Gebremichael, as regional president, effectively setting up a rival political authority to the interim administration established under the Pretoria agreement. The TPLF accused the federal government of failing to honour its side of the deal.

Federal and Tigrayan forces then clashed at Shererina, near the Sudanese border, on August 1. Heavy artillery and drones were used in the fighting, and hundreds of Tigrayans, including wounded fighters, fled into Sudan.

On August 20, two drones struck homes in Mekelle, wounding 13 people, according to the TPLF. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the account.

On September 20, a drone destroyed a truck carrying 41 tonnes of food aid near Adi Daero, according to the TPLF. Addis Ababa has acknowledged none of the reported strikes.

“We signed the Pretoria Agreement, but the regime used the agreement to kill the people of Tigray systematically,” the TPLF’s spokesperson, Michael Asgedom, told Al Jazeera.

The alliance “was created to bring peace and democracy to Ethiopia”, he said.

He also said it would build a new order “over the ruins of Abiy Ahmed’s system” and that this was “the right time to eradicate the regime”.

If war comes, he said, “it will be for survival.”

One script is for diplomats, the other for fighters.

Tronvoll calls it constructive ambiguity, a phrase that fits the alliance.

That the alliance claims to speak for seven peoples can delegitimise Abiy abroad and raise the price of any settlement, whether or not it fires a shot.

The first test is Eritrea, the neighbour whose name appears nowhere in the founding statement.

Over the past two years, Eritrea has reconciled with the TPLF, the enemy its troops helped to crush in 2020, as Abiy began demanding access to the Red Sea, which Asmara interpreted as a claim on its coast.

Jawar argues that Eritrea’s minimum aim is to keep any conflict on the Ethiopian side of the border.

The International Crisis Group has similarly assessed that Eritrea wants to establish a buffer zone on its southern border.

Asgedom has denied any Eritrean military presence in Tigray, but left the door ajar.

“If Eritrea can take action because of a potential danger to its survival, it is the Eritreans who should answer that question.”

Tronvoll says Eritrean troops are in Tigray now, a claim Al Jazeera could not independently verify. Magnus Taylor, deputy director of the International Crisis Group’s Horn of Africa project, told Al Jazeera that he was more cautious.

“This is substantially a domestic Ethiopian phenomenon,” he said.

The second test is whether seven commands can fight as one.

Zemene chairs the alliance, but the founding statement names no commander for a joint campaign.

If the line ever advances on Addis Ababa, Tronvoll asks, whose soldiers go first?

“If it is a Tigrayan general commanding Amharas to be sacrificed first to save the Tigrayan soldiers, that will split it immediately.”

Western Tigray is not mentioned in the statement either.

Taylor says the Fano are themselves divided over it: Commanders in Gojjam and Wollo can contemplate an alliance with Tigray, while those nearer the disputed land cannot.

“All these groups have their own different beef with the federal government,” Taylor said, and much of it dates from Abiy’s first year.

In 2018, Abiy invited exiled rebels home, and the OLA and the ONLF returned from Asmara.

But the OLA broke away to keep fighting, and talks with it in Tanzania collapsed in 2023.

The ONLF then split in 2025 after its then-chairman called for a return to armed struggle amid a dispute over a Chinese natural-gas concession in the Somali region.

The Amharan Fano rebelled against the government in 2023 after Abiy ordered the regional special forces to be folded into the federal army, a move many Amhara believed was tantamount to disarmament.

In June, Abiy’s Prosperity Party won 438 of 486 contested parliamentary seats. Voting did not take place in Tigray and was disrupted by insecurity in parts of Amhara and Oromia.

But their grievances are not only with Abiy’s government.

Referring to the news of the alliance, Jawar said he had “not seen anything as unpopular among the Oromos”, after years of accusations that Fano fighters have killed Oromo civilians in Wollega.

The OLA calls its participation a “procedural consensus” and has demanded that Fano disown a faction in Wollega that it says the government armed.

“There is no shared political objective,” Jawar said. “They don’t even have a shared tactical objective.”

And Tronvoll goes further: “If the members ever reached the palace, immediately a new war will start between them.”

Then, there are the people being asked to fight.

Tigrayans are being mobilised alongside forces they remember from four years ago, when, in Tronvoll’s characterisation, “both the Eritreans and the Fano Amharas were perpetrating genocide on them.”

Friends in Tigray have told Tronvoll of coercive recruitment. He estimates that tens of thousands have left the region in advance of a possible war and the draft.

“People are voting with their feet,” he said. “They are on their knees already. So what are the alternatives for them than to fight?”

“As long as they don’t threaten the palace at Arat Kilo, he can live with that,” Tronvoll said. “I don’t think he skips lunch because of this.”

“Is it a headache? Is it an irritant? Is it a blow? It’s a combination of those things.”

In his assessment, the TPLF, which lost most of its heavy weapons in 2022, has come off worse in recent clashes against federal air power. The likelier course, he says, is a slow deterioration, with southern Tigray the flashpoint.

Jawar views Abiy’s approach as containment: Keep flights into Tigray running so that those who want to leave can do so, and let a war that few want sour public opinion.

With Tigrayan forces having seized Mekelle’s airport, that exit has closed.

Tom Gardner, author of The Abiy Project, said, “For months Abiy’s strategy has been to maintain a low-level conflict largely conducted via drones, proxies, and siege tactics. This could be the moment that strategy breaks down and a full-scale war erupts.”

The regional dimension is becoming harder to separate from the conflict inside Ethiopia.

The International Crisis Group says several thousand Tigrayans, mostly from Western Tigray/Welkait, have fought alongside the Sudanese army against the Rapid Support Forces.

Khartoum has also accused Addis Ababa of allowing drones to strike Sudan from Ethiopian soil, which Ethiopia denies.

Eritrea has aligned itself with Sudan’s army and established ties with Egypt, an opponent of Addis Ababa in the dispute surrounding Nile water resources.

The International Crisis Group has described Egypt as a close wartime ally of the Sudanese army.

Those alignments do not necessarily make the new Ethiopian alliance a regional military bloc. But they make it harder to treat Ethiopia’s conflicts as entirely domestic.

In Mekelle, the calculation is narrower.

“It is better to live than to die,” Asgedom said, “and the regime doesn’t allow us to live.”

A journalist in Mekelle, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said people had lived for months in a state of no-war-no-peace, and many now wanted it decided either way.

The alliance offers a path to war without making clear what that war would cost.

“We need peace,” residents told the journalist in Mekelle, after months without salaries or medicine.

In the city, there is an old belief that an unexpectedly windy and sunny day foretells fighting. Tuesday was both.

articles.title: Zelensky defends attacks on Russian refineries: ‘Our lives are more important than the price of energy’
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky declared “our lives are more important than the price of energy” in an interview while defending his strikes against Russian oil refineries. Speaking with the Wall Street Journal’s editor-in-chief Emma Tucker on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Zelensky responded when asked if President Trump pressed the Ukrainian President…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky declared “our lives are more important than the price of energy” in an interview while defending his strikes against Russian oil refineries.

Speaking with the Wall Street Journal’s editor-in-chief Emma Tucker on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Zelensky responded when asked if President Trump pressed the Ukrainian President to cease strikes against Russian oil refineries amid growing diesel prices globally.

“Today we didn’t talk about it, but by phone, yes… we were at this topic about the diesel,” Zelensky said. “I said, look… our lives are more important than the price of energy.”

Zelensky said in the interview that he would only stop strikes if a ceasefire were established with Moscow. He later posted on social media that Kyiv is “ready for an energy ceasefire if they do not attack our energy system, our electricity, heating, and water supply” but that he was unsure if Russia was ready for this proposal.

Ukraine launched attacks on a refinery in Siberia on Thursday, creating fuel shortages in Russia and prompting Moscow to retaliate on urban gas stations. One attack focused on the city of Nizhnekamsk, which is the home of several key oil refineries, while another drone attack hit a crucial refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Russia’s Krasnodar region near Crimea.

Trump has blamed the attacks as a major reason global diesel prices soared this week with the average price of diesel sitting at $6.27 on Tuesday – the highest ever. Diesel is a primary fuel source for public transportation and the trucking industry and rising prices are expected to push up the cost of goods.

The president urged Zelensky earlier this month, “to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.”

“There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting, that’s hurting the world,” Trump added.

Russian forces escalated its campaign against Ukraine with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones striking Ukraine’s power grid ahead of the harsh winter season.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia in a statement of “systematically attacking places” where people frequent in order to “maximize casualties, spread fear, and put pressure on Ukrainian society.”

articles.title: Russia’s attacks on Ukraine kill six after Zelenskyy-Trump talks
articles.summary: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy met Trump on Tuesday and discussed a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets.
articles.body:
At least two people have been killed in Ukraine’s capital Kyiv, along with four others in the front-line Donetsk region, as Russia pounds the country just hours after US President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed peace efforts.

The rare daytime attack on Kyiv was carried out with faster and high-flying jet drones that are harder to intercept and lasted for hours from the morning into early afternoon on Wednesday, killing two and injuring more than 30 others, according to local officials.

Zelenskyy said Russia had deployed many drones against the city, with a large number of them jet-powered.

“Russia continues to turn civilian and critical infrastructure into targets: pharmaceutical facilities, ‌gas stations, railways, communications infrastructure, and shopping malls,” he said on X.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a Russian drone hit a nine-storey non-residential building in his city, as well as a business centre and warehouses.

Ukrainian oil company Ukrnafta said Russia hit one of its petrol stations in the capital, the sixth such facility attacked in recent weeks. In total, two petrol stations came ‌under attack, authorities said.

The chief executive of the Ukrainian railway operator, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, said railway infrastructure in the capital was also attacked and that one of its workers was injured.

A separate Russian aerial bomb attack killed at least four people and injured four others in a village in the front-line Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, the regional governor said on Telegram.

On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Zelenskyy met Trump on Tuesday and discussed a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets. He asked for increased supplies of US Patriot air defence missiles to defend the country against an expected increase in Russian attacks on energy infrastructure during winter.

The Ukrainian leader added that no agreements were reached but that he was ready for “any format” of an energy ceasefire with Russia as long as it stopped its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure.

On Monday, the Financial Times newspaper reported, citing people familiar with the call, that Trump pressed Zelenskyy on Sunday to halt Kyiv’s strikes on Russian refineries over concerns that the attacks are exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up prices.

Still on Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters before a meeting between US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that there were no grounds for peace talks with Ukraine.

“For now, there are no prerequisites for moving onto a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks,” Peskov said.

He added that President Vladimir Putin was ready to meet Trump one-on-one if the leaders felt it was necessary. Still, he reiterated that any Putin-Zelenskyy meeting would require the Ukrainian leader to go to Moscow.

Ukraine has previously said going to Moscow for any talks was unacceptable and that any talks must be held in a neutral country.

The spokesperson added that it was not the right time for a peace summit either. “Generally speaking, in any other circumstances, it would be inappropriate to hold a summit meeting before the groundwork has been laid at expert level, as this would be a waste of time,” he said.

articles.title: Row over AI caricatures of west London councillor
articles.summary: Labour's Sital Punja says the cartoons contain "racist tropes" - something the Conservatives reject.
articles.body:
A west London councillor has called for stronger protections for elected officials after AI-generated caricatures depicting her were posted on social media by the local Conservative Party.

Sital Punja, a Labour member of Tory-controlled Hillingdon Council, said the images using AI to manipulate her likeness contained "racist and antisemitic tropes".

One cartoon image posted by the Hillingdon Conservatives on X showed Punja, who is of Indian descent, controlling white male counterparts as puppets.

The Hillingdon Conservative Group rejected the allegations, stating the images were intended strictly as "political satire", and denied any racist or antisemitic intent.

"It was the racism. And I don't accept that they think it's political satire," Punja told BBC London.

"Puppeteering tropes have been used as antisemitic and racist tropes for years - for decades, for a very long time.

"As Labour Party members, we get antisemitic training to ensure our awareness of what is antisemitic, and tropes like these are used in our training so that we have awareness of that."

Another AI-generated cartoon shared by the local Conservative account showed Punja running past horse-drawn carts bearing slogans criticising Labour policies.

She said: "Political satire is bouncing off policies... it doesn't mean you have to have a brown woman controlling white men, running off with money on the backdrop of finances going down.

"The portrayal of me had exaggerated features, making me look like the menace that you want me to look like."

Punja, who used to be the Labour group's deputy leader, said a wider campaign of online abuse had taken a severe toll on her health.

"From July last year, it had become extremely toxic as a female politician," she said. "Race and gender had to play a part in why people were attacking me.

"Having been subjected to this, I really do think about it now. I've had to go to the police, I've had to talk to my children about safety, and people don't realise the impact it has on your mental health."

She added: "To tell me - who has been beaten up on the streets as a young child for the colour of my skin - that I don't know what racism feels like, is appalling."

The Hillingdon Conservative Group denied the posts were racist, antisemitic or misogynistic, describing them as "political satire relating to Councillor Punja's position and former influence".

"We completely reject any antisemitic references or claims relating to this," the group's spokesperson said.

"It was merely a reference to Councillor Punja 'pulling the strings' of her colleagues at the time when she was deputy leader of Hillingdon Labour."

They added local Labour branches had also posted AI-manipulated images of Conservative members online, citing posts showing Tory councillors alongside a gameshow wheel and "closed" signs on local services.

Punja said these accounts were not associated with her and were not the same as the Hillingdon Labour group posting them.

Dr Ben Gidley, an academic at Birkbeck University's Institute for the Study of Antisemitism, said politicians should be careful when using AI to create images.

While declining to comment on the specific Hillingdon dispute, Gidley noted the "puppet master" motif had deep historical roots in antisemitic propaganda, warning that AI image tools risk "intensifying the use of racist imagery" by drawing on vast datasets of historical prejudice.

He said in recent years, far-right social media accounts had applied similar imagery to target other minority groups in addition to Jews.

"Social media has really accelerated the speed at which misinformation, caricatures, stereotypes get circulated," he said.

"It's sped up the ways in which that reservoir of hostile ideas kind of circulates."

Why fake AI videos of UK urban decline are taking over social media

AI fake nearly led to serious disorder, says Khan

Punja said she had reported the images posted by the Conservatives to Hillingdon Council's Standards Committee and called for local government rules to be modernised.

"I would like to see our members' code of conduct upgraded to incorporate social media, and more legislation around AI images," she said.

"Once those images go into AI systems, an image of me will be characterised in that way forever."

Punja said she remained committed to her role in local government.

"If I stop, they've won," she said. "A diverse, inclusive society means that we need to have all types of people around the table and all voices heard."

Hillingdon Council said it had a recognised complaints process and would not comment on individual allegations.

articles.title: Chris Spatola, ESPN college basketball analyst, dies suddenly at 47
articles.summary: ESPN college basketball analyst Chris Spatola, the son-in-law of legendary coach Mike Krzyzewski, died suddenly, triggering a flood of tributes for the former West Point guard and Army combat veteran.
articles.body: ESPN college basketball analyst Chris Spatola died suddenly, network officials said Tuesday, triggering a flood of tributes for the former West Point guard and Army combat veteran. The network did not reveal how Spatola — the son-in-law of all-time college basketball coaching wins leader Mike Krzyzewski — died, only saying that he had “passed away unexpectedly Monday.” He was 47. “Chris Spatola brought a unique perspective to ESPN’s college basketball coverage, shaped by his experiences as a student-athlete, Army veteran, coach and broadcaster,” according to an ESPN statement. “He was thoughtful, prepared and passionate about the sport, earning the respect of colleagues, coaches, players and fans alike,” the network said. “We extend our heartfelt condolences to his loved ones during this difficult time.” Spatola had been with ESPN since 2015, following a distinguished career on the basketball floor and battlefield. “I am devastated over the passing of my friend and colleague Chris Spatola. Chris was a wonderful human being,” fellow ESPN college basketball analyst Jay Bilas said in a statement. “With Chris, it was never about him, it was only about the game, the players, the coaches, and the fans,” Bilas said. “Heartbroken beyond words to lose such a great friend, yet grateful beyond words to have known him.” Spatola is the the 10th leading scorer in Army history, contributing 1,543 points over 111 games (13.9 ppg) between 1998 and 2002. He’s No. 4 on the career Army list for 3-pointers, sinking 238 of his 637 long-range tries (37%). “Devastated to hear the news of the loss of Chris Spatola,” ESPN broadcaster Rece Davis said in a statement. “Brilliant, funny, dedicated to his family, hoops and his crafts of coaching and broadcasting.” Following that illustrious career at West Point, Spatola was active duty from 2002 to 2007, which included a tour during Operation Iraqi Freedom, ESPN said. Spatola stepped out of fatigues and back on to the hardwood as an assistant coach for Duke basketball between 2007 and 2012. The Blue Devils cut down the nets in 2010, led that season in scoring by current head coach Jon Scheyer. Spatola and his wife, Jamie Krzyzewski Spatola, have three children. “We are deeply saddened by the passing of Chris Spatola,” according to a Duke basketball statement. “Chris was a beloved Army veteran, coach, broadcaster, and true friend to the Duke Basketball family. We send our love and condolences to his wife Jamie and three children, the Spatola and Krzyzewski families, and everyone who loved him.”

articles.title: Gary Anderson: On-the-run killer arrested in Donegal
articles.summary: Gary Anderson, who has been unlawfully at large for over a week, has been arrested in the Republic of Ireland.
articles.body:
A man who was convicted of murder and has been unlawfully at large for over a week has been arrested in the Republic of Ireland.

Gary Anderson, 29, was jailed for life in 2023, alongside his brother, for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry .

He was on temporary release from prison to attend his father's funeral when he absconded.

He was arrested on Wednesday by An Garda Síochána (Irish police) at a property in the town of Buncrana in County Donegal.

Karol Kelly's sister had said the family felt "let down" by the justice system after learning that he was on the run.

The Justice Minister, Naomi Long, welcomed Anderson's arrest.

She said she hopes the arrest "goes some way towards alleviating the anxiety and uncertainty" that Karol Kelly's family have experienced.

Long is due to meet the family later this week.

She added that she recognises that "questions remain about the circumstances surrounding" Anderson's release and abscondment.

"Work is progressing to establish an independent review, and further details will be announced shortly."

The circumstances surrounding Anderson's release sparked a political row in Northern Ireland, with Long denying on Monday that she had misled the assembly over the matter.

MP for Foyle, Colum Eastwood, welcomed Anderson's arrest and said "confidence has been damaged in the institutions involved".

Anderson failed to return to prison on 14 September and was last seen in the Eastway area of Derry.

Det Insp Gareth Lavery of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) thanked "everyone who assisted with our enquiries since our public appeal last Monday".

He added that officers "conducted extensive enquiries during this investigation to locate Gary Anderson".

Lavery also thanked An Garda Síochána officers "who arrested Gary Anderson today and for all of their help with this investigation over the last week".

"PSNI is now working with relevant authorities in order to return Gary Anderson to custody, and we will provide an update in due course."

An Garda Síochána asid they arrested a man, aged in his 20s, in Donegal as "part of a planned operation".

"He is being detained under the provisions of Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984, at a station in the Garda North Western Region."

Buncrana is about a 20-minute drive from the Irish border.

The town is popular with visitors from the north-west of Northern Ireland.

articles.title: Jaishankar-Rubio meeting: India flags sanctions, US waves friendship
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: In a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday with US secretary of state Marco Rubio, India’s
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: In a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday with US secretary of state Marco Rubio, India’s external affairs minister S Jaishankar raised New Delhi’s “interests and concerns” over Washington’s newly enacted Russia sanctions legislation, exposing a widening rift between the two sides even as the US publicly sought to portray the relationship as firmly on track.The difference in their post-meeting social media messaging was striking. Jaishankar's account was unusually specific: the sanctions legislation was the first issue he mentioned, alongside the Gulf and Ukraine. Rubio's post on X made no reference to the sanctions issue. Instead, he wrote: “Great to meet with Indian External Affairs Minister @DrSJaishankar in New York today,” saying the two were “building on the US-India strategic partnership” and coordinating on regional priorities and upcoming multilateral efforts.The diplomatic gloss barely concealed the widening gap after New Delhi bluntly warned Washington last week that using the new sanctions authority against India could affect bilateral relations. The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA), which President Donald Trump signed last week, gives him authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. India, which is one, has said it remains committed to securing affordable energy for its 1.4 billion people and will take measures to protect its economic interests.There is also an increasingly awkward optics problem for Washington. Analysts have pointed to the US exemption allowing continued Russian uranium imports for itself even as Washington threatens punitive measures against other countries buying Russian energy. The US imported or used substantial Russian-origin enrichment services in 2025, while Washington has been scrambling to build alternative domestic capacity.Former US official and South Asia analyst Evan Feigenbaum has similarly highlighted what he sees as a double standard in Washington's pressure on India, particularly after Trump announced that the US was exploring a deal to buy potash from Belarus, a close Russian ally. Trump has defended the proposal as a way to obtain cheaper fertilizer for American farmers.Meanwhile, in further signs that Trump’s actions -- regarded as whimsical by critics -- are hurting Americans as much as the rest of the world, US diesel prices have crossed $6.50 a gallon nationally (approx Rs 165 per liter), adding costs for farmers, truckers and virtually every part of the agricultural supply chain. The administration is now scrambling to restrict diesel exports amid tanking poll numbers for Trump.Indian officials likewise have repeatedly emphasised that energy decisions will be based on national interests and economic considerations, ignoring abrasive rhetoric from some US lawmakers. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a principal architect of the sanctions legislation, warned India and China during the congressional debate to “clean up your act” and buy their oil and gas elsewhere.The emerging tension is particularly notable against the backdrop of Washington's elaborate courtship of Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in the US on Wednesday for a three-day state visit, with Trump personally scheduled to greet him at Joint Base Andrews -- a rare gesture -- and a full state arrival ceremony and White House state dinner planned for Thursday.The spectacle underscores the asymmetry in the relationships: Washington is literally pawing the ground and playing doggo before Beijing even as it is willing to risk friction with New Delhi. The Jaishankar-Rubio meeting meanwhile offered a revealing snapshot of an increasingly complicated US-India partnership -- one in which the language of strategic cooperation is becoming harder to reconcile with the increasingly contentious economic component of the relationship.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran president tells UN ‘we will never bow our head’ as US walks out
articles.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian projected defiance in his speech at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, saying the Islamic Republic would not surrender or give up its nuclear program in the face of President Trump’s military and economic pressure. “He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the…
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian projected defiance in his speech at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, saying the Islamic Republic would not surrender or give up its nuclear program in the face of President Trump’s military and economic pressure.

“He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying,” Pezeshkian told the room. The U.S. representative had earlier walked out of the Iranian president’s speech.

Pezeshkian’s speech came after Trump told the global body that Tehran faces a choice of either striking a deal with the U.S. to end the more than six-month war or facing “annihilation.”

“We will never bow our head or bend at the knee,” Pezeshkian continued.

“Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force.”

Referencing Trump’s threats to wipe out Iran, he said, “everything uttered about our country goes against the very essence and charter and the spirit of the United Nations.”

The Iranian president further reiterated Iran’s position that it does not seek a nuclear weapon, but that it rejects constraints on its pursuit of nuclear technology.

“We say it clearly: No nuclear weapons and no limitations to peaceful nuclear technology,” he said.

The U.N.’s nuclear watchdog earlier this month reported Iran to the U.N. Security Council for noncompliance with its nuclear safeguard agreements, the first instance of such a censure in 20 years.

In September 2025, the Security Council triggered a snapback of sanctions on Iran in the face of restrictions on monitoring its nuclear program and deadlock in negotiations with the U.S. at the time.

Trump has said his war against Iran is centered on preventing the Islamic Republic from developing a nuclear weapon, but a sweeping military operation and economic pressure campaign have so far failed to force Iran’s capitulation. Tehran has succeeded in holding the global energy market hostage and inflicting economic pain, especially in the U.S., with rising gas and diesel prices.

Trump predicted that Iran will come to an agreement with the U.S. after the midterm elections, suggesting they are waiting to see if he winds up in a weakened position in the event Republicans lose their majorities in the House and Senate.

“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran,” Trump said in his speech to the U.N.

Trump’s envoys for negotiations, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, held indirect talks with Iranian officials on Tuesday on the sidelines of the global summit.

Witkoff said he hopes the “lengthy” talks “will prove constructive and promising” in a post on the social platform X.

articles.title: IIT-Bombay suicide case: New CCTV footage shows Sahil Wakode’s movements before he left exam hall
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The city Crime Branch probing the abetment to suicide of IIT Bombay second-year student Sahil Wakode has collected CCTV footage showing his
articles.body: MUMBAI: The city Crime Branch probing the abetment to suicide of IIT Bombay second-year student Sahil Wakode has collected CCTV footage showing his movements during the examination in which he was allegedly caught copying.According to investigators, footage from September 18 shows Wakode inside the examination hall between around 12.30 pm and 12.45 pm, when the semester examination was nearing its end.The footage allegedly shows him bending down and looking at a mobile phone kept in his pocket. Police are examining the allegation that he was using ChatGPT to answer questions during the examination.The footage then shows the invigilator noticing Wakode’s movements and approaching him. The invigilator is seen taking his answer sheet and asking the student to follow him out of the examination hall.The footage shows Sahil getting up, collecting his belongings and preparing to leave. articles.title: A Georgia property began as a military academy summer camp; after 30 years as one family's retreat, the 280-acre estate with a 10-acre lake and six miles of trails is asking $7.5 million
articles.summary: A property once filled with the regimented routines of a military academy summer camp has taken on a very different rhythm.
articles.body: A property once filled with the regimented routines of a military academy summer camp has taken on a very different rhythm. According to a report by the Mansion Global, in Chattahoochee Hills, Georgia, a sprawling 280-acre estate known as Camp David has spent the past three decades as a private family retreat, where summers revolved around horses, hiking, fishing and long days outdoors. Now, the expansive property is on the market for $7.5 million. Scroll down to read the details of the property.From summer camp to family retreatAs per Mansion Global report, the estate was originally owned by the Georgia Military Academy, which was renamed Woodward Academy in 1966. In the early 1960s, the property operated as a summer camp with tightly scheduled days that began with reveille and ended with lights out at 9:30 p.m. And camp activities included arts and crafts, field games, archery and campfire gatherings, giving generations of students a structured outdoor escape. Decades later, the same land became a much more informal gathering place for one Atlanta-area family.The grandparents of current co-listing agent Ashley Altenbach purchased the property and gradually expanded it by acquiring additional acreage from neighboring landowners. Over 30 years, Camp David evolved into a multigenerational retreat where their 10 grandchildren regularly spent holidays and extended summer visits.A private estate built for outdoor livingAs per the online report, the centerpiece of the property is a custom-built three-bedroom, three-bathroom main residence. A renovated guesthouse adds three bedrooms and two bathrooms, while a historic two-bedroom cottage provides another potential living or rental space. Beyond the residences, the estate is designed around recreation and open space. A 10-acre stocked lake provides opportunities for fishing and kayaking, while roughly six miles of riding and hiking trails wind through mature forests and pastures.The grounds also feature a large swimming pool, a three-stall horse barn with a riding ring and former football and baseball fields. A sizable gymnasium has since been converted into garage and storage space, preserving another reminder of the property's earlier life.A rare estate near AtlantaAccording to Mansion Global, Chattahoochee Hills sits about 25 miles southwest of Atlanta and was incorporated in 2007. The city developed around sustainability-focused planning principles, including restrictions intended to preserve open land and limit the intensity of development. Camp David sits directly across from Serenbe, the well-known sustainable community centered around a main street of shops and gathering spaces. The estate's history is also tied to the formation of Chattahoochee Hills, with the former owner among the city's founding members.That combination of scale, history and proximity to Atlanta makes the property unusual. Large private estates are increasingly difficult to find within easy reach of the city, particularly those offering extensive trails, water frontage, equestrian facilities and multiple residences, adds the online report.After serving as a military academy camp and then a cherished family getaway for 30 years, Camp David is now entering its next chapter with 280 acres of Georgia landscape, a 10-acre lake and a remarkable collection of recreational amenities offered for $7.5 million.Images Courtesy: Mansion GlobalReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
articles.summary: Poland says the aircraft stayed in its skies for 42 seconds, forcing the Nato member to scramble its fighter jets.
articles.body:
Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.

Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.

It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.

Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.

By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.

Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect

In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.

Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.

A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.

Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.

"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said.

"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."

Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.

These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.

Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd".

Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure".

articles.title: Ladakh withdraws cases against 20 booked in Leh violence; Sonam Wangchuk leads padyatra ahead of anniversary
articles.summary: LEH: On the eve of the first anniversary of the violence in Leh that left four people dead, Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena on Wednesday
articles.body: LEH: On the eve of the first anniversary of the violence in Leh that left four people dead, Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena on Wednesday announced the withdrawal of criminal cases against 20 people booked in connection with the incident.Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk also led a symbolic padyatra in the city to demand justice for those killed and injured.Saxena said the decision was taken after a comprehensive review, with the Ladakh Police recommending a closure report for the 20 individuals in FIR No 144/2005 registered at the Leh police station under Section 360 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), news agency PTI reported.“In the larger interest of peace, public tranquillity, and social harmony in Ladakh, I have approved the withdrawal of criminal cases against 20 individuals, related to the unfortunate violence that erupted in Leh on September 24 last year,” Saxena said in a post on X.He said the decision would allow the 20 individuals to move forward with their lives and careers, adding that prioritising justice and healing over prolonged litigation would help foster a peaceful and harmonious society in Ladakh.Saxena also thanked Union home minister Amit Shah for his “constant guidance and sympathetic approach” in matters concerning victims and their families.The announcement came a day after representatives of the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) met officials of the Ministry of Home Affairs in Leh, as the region prepared to mark the first anniversary of the violence.Meanwhile, Wangchuk, a member of the LAB, led the padyatra ahead of Thursday’s Shaheed Diwas, which will mark one year since the September 24, 2025 violence during protests demanding statehood and Sixth Schedule safeguards for Ladakh.The march was shortened due to changing weather conditions, while organisers kept the programme local and limited participation from outside the region. The padyatra also saw limited participation from local people, PTI reported.“We organised the padyatra today and will observe Shaheed Diwas tomorrow in memory of those who were killed in the indiscriminate firing on September 24 last year. The day will be observed as Shaheed Diwas, with people expected to offer prayers at temples, mosques, churches and other religious places,” Wangchuk said.He demanded that the report of the judicial inquiry into the September 24 incident be submitted at the earliest, saying a year had passed without its findings being made public.Wangchuk said the inquiry should establish the circumstances that led to the firing, whether there was an order to open fire and how the violence began. He also sought adequate compensation for those killed and injured.The September 24, 2025 protests in Leh, held over demands for statehood and Sixth Schedule safeguards for Ladakh, turned violent, leaving four people dead and several others injured, PTI reported.The Union Territory administration subsequently ordered a judicial inquiry into the circumstances leading to the violence and police action.The LAB and KDA have since been engaged in talks with the Centre over Ladakh’s demands.Wangchuk said the next meeting with the Centre is scheduled for October and urged the government to address the issues with “an open heart, a clear mind and honesty”.Wangchuk further added that September was being observed as “martyrs’ month” in memory of those who died, were injured or jailed during the agitation for safeguards for Ladakh’s land, culture and democratic rights.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. articles.title: 150 Brechin homes damaged by Storm Babet flooding in 2023 to be demolished
articles.summary: Residents in Brechin say they have been living in limbo since floods in 2023.
articles.body:
A total of 150 homes in an Angus town which were devastated by Storm Babet almost three years ago are to be demolished.

Hundreds of people who fled their homes when the South Esk breached flood defences in the River Street area of Brechin were unable to return for months and many properties remain empty.

Councillors have approved plans to demolish 150 houses and flats, plus five garages, as well as changes to the river's flood defences that could cost about £8.2m.

Residents said they had been living in limbo since the floods hit in October 2023.

Dozens of storm-damaged houses could be demolished

Council says Storm Babet repairs will exceed £4m

Who pays the bills after the Storm Babet flooding?

Storm Babet brought very strong winds and heavy rain across much of Scotland and north-east England.

The Met Office recorded up eight inches (200mm) of rainfall in the wettest areas.

Angus was one of the worst affected places. In Brechin, 60 households had to be rescued and many more went to evacuation centres in Montrose and Forfar.

'Why should I bother doing up the house?'

Betty Matheson, 78, was forced out of her privately-rented home and was unable to return for several months while the house was gutted, rewired and restored.

She said: "I think for all of us still living round here it's been like living in limbo.

"There are things I would like to do to the house, but should I bother?

"What is the point of doing something to the house and the house is going to be taken down? So there is this uncertainty all about it."

She said she would miss the area, but knew her family would help her settle in a new place if needed.

"I think it's a shame for Brechin itself," she told BBC Scotland.

But she added: "I think I've known for a long time that I will have to move, but I am pragmatic about it."

Angus Council held a special meeting to consider options for the future of damaged homes, and the flood defences.

Ahead of the meeting, councillor George Meechan said the local authority recognised how difficult the continuing uncertainty had been for residents.

"Unfortunately, there is no simple solution that will meet everyone's needs in this area, and councillors must carefully consider the impact on wider Angus communities also affected by climate change," he said.

Councillors have agreed to demolish a total of 150 homes, including 29 that are in private ownership.

Local Brechin councillor and deputy provost, Jill Scott, said the council knew that not everyone would be happy with the decision.

But she said it would "bring closure" for affected households.

"With today's decision, the residents and council officers now have clarity in the next steps and while there is a lot of work to do, and there remain some risks in progressing this option, we can move forward together," she said.

"I also want to stress that no-one is going to be made homeless by this decision. Our housing officers will support anyone into their next home, whether they are council tenants, private tenants or homeowners."

Another affected resident said she wondered why Angus Council had taken so long to act since the storm.

Stella McIntosh, 82, has lived in the home she owns on River Street for the past 45 years.

The water reached shoulder-height in her house, but she has learned to live with the loss of irreplaceable belongings damaged or washed away in the flood.

She said she believed her house could fall within the preferred option area for demolition.

While her home was renovated after Storm Babet, other properties have remained empty, leaving the area like a "ghost town".

"I just feel at my age I don't want to have to move again, but we're going to have absolutely no option," she added.

John Cavanagh, who lives behind River Street on Mitchell Drive, has concerns even though his home is not earmarked for demolition.

He had to be taken by boat from his house during the storm.

"This whole area was a pond - it was deep enough to take a motorboat fortunately," he said.

"We were extremely lucky. I've got no explanation for why we didn't get water in the house at all."

He has sympathy for those whose homes were damaged and is also worried that if there was a repeat of the floods the remaining houses could be affected.

"Will the flood defences work next time, should they be adjusted?" he asked.

"What's going to happen 50, 60, 100 years from now? We need to plan that.

"Leaving things as they are clearly didn't work during the floods. If anything, some people will tell us the climate has worsened and we can expect more of these floods."

Angus Council has proposed raising the height of the current flood wall.

It said the outline cost was about £8.2m.

Plaintiff Allie Coghan told Fox News Digital that she hopes the appeal will establish a clear legal precedent that protects single-sex private spaces and keeps national organizations from overriding local member consent. articles.title: Badenoch registers gift of £8,177 for Murdoch meeting
articles.summary: The Murdochs' News Corp company paid for flights and accommodation for the Conservative leader and her husband to travel to Greece.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has registered gifts worth £8,177 covering travel and accommodation for a meeting with media mogul Rupert Murdoch in Greece.

Badenoch, along with her husband Hamish and shadow minister Alex Burghart, were flown to Athens on 24 August - with the costs paid for by the Murdoch family's News Corp UK organisation.

Badenoch's spokesperson said: "Kemi was pleased to meet Rupert Murdoch and senior News Corp and News UK executives.

"The visit has been declared in full in the usual way."

The spokesperson added: "Kemi values serious engagement with Britain's major media organisations and the people who run them (including at the BBC) and will continue to make the case for a free and independent press."

The figures were published in the latest register of members' financial interests, in which MPs must report gifts worth more than £300 within 28 days of receipt.

In the latest list, Prime Minister Andy Burnham registered three tickets worth £677.34 for seats in the directors' lounge at Everton's first game of the Premier League season.

In the record of her meeting with Murdoch, Badenoch lists the following gifts for her and her husband from News Corp UK:

An outbound flight from Rome to Athens and a return flight to London, amounting to an estimated value of £4,000

Ground transportation and transfers costing £1,752.50

She describes the purpose of the visit as an "off-site meetings with Mr K R Murdoch and other senior executives from News Corp and News UK".

Burghart, the Conservative shadow Northern Ireland secretary, also attended the meeting and has registered a gift of £4,088.97, covering flights, accommodation and transportation.

The meeting took place shortly after Badenoch met Italian Prime Minister Georgia Meloni in Italy.

Badenoch previously met Murdoch, along with other News Corp executives in 2022, when she was an international trade minister.

Murdoch stepped down as News Corp chair in 2023 transitioning to the role of chairman emeritus.

His son Lachlan became chair of the company, which owns UK media organisations including Virgin Radio, TalkSPORT, and the newspapers the Sun and the Times.

UK politicians over the years have sought to develop good relationships with Murdoch and in 2011 Labour's Tony Blair became godfather to his daughter.

Murdoch's publications have switched political allegiances throughout the decades, backing the Conservatives in the 1980s and early 90s and switching to Labour in 1997, before returning to the Conservatives in 2010.

In 2024, the Sunday Times and the Sun endorsed Sir Keir Starmer's Labour Party.

articles.title: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'
articles.summary: Masoud Pezeshkian's defiant speech to the UN comes after the US president threatened to "annihilate" Iran if a peace deal is not agreed soon.
articles.body:
President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Iran will never "bend the knee" after almost seven months of war with the US and Israel, but is ready for a diplomatic solution to the conflict.

Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, he told the UN General Assembly: "The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying."

Pezeshkian also insisted any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using a key Gulf waterway.

"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access," he said.

There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address.

US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat

American power, AI and a walkout - key moments from Trump's UN speech

UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes

"The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York.

He then held up a photo of the country's late Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike on his residence when the US and Israel launched a joint attack in late February.

He also presented pictures of some of the more than 175 civilians, two thirds of them children, who Iranian authorities say were killed in missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd that day. The US has denied striking Lamerd and said it is still investigating what happened in Minab.

"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed on our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said.

Also on Wednesday, an attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz killed an Indian sailor, the Agence France-Presse news agency reported, citing Omani and Indian authorities.

The attack was condemned by India's foreign ministry, which called for unimpeded passage through the Strait to be restored.

In February, Iran retaliated for the massive US-Israeli air campaign by launching deadly missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.

It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, by attacking commercial vessels in the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The US responded by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports and ships in April.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran wants to retain some measure of control over the strait and collect fees from vessels that use it, which the US has rejected.

In his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a "big decision" - either negotiate a deal that would allow Iranians to rebuild their country, or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".

Pezeshkian said the threat was "a sign of a bullying mentality".

"[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend the knee," he said.

But he added: "We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force."

Pezeshkian made clear that the US blockade would have to end as part of any deal.

"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway," he said.

He also reiterated that Iran would not give up its right to have a civilian nuclear programme and that it would not seek to develop nuclear weapons.

"We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons and no limitations on peaceful nuclear technology."

Trump argued in his speech that the war had prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb and demanded that its leaders "relinquish their nuclear ambitions".

On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Witkoff said he hoped the discussions – the first since June – would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work.

But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

articles.title: Michael Kiwanuka: Singer reveals he is recovering from a stroke
articles.summary: The award-winning musician says he faces a "tough journey ahead" after a "quite severe" brain injury.
articles.body:
Award-winning singer-songwriter Michael Kiwanuka has revealed he has suffered a stroke and faces a "long, tough journey ahead" to recover.

The 39-year-old from London, who won the Mercury Prize in 2020 and has been nominated for five Brit Awards, said in an Instagram post that the stroke occurred "a few months ago" and was caused "by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure".

He added that "the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done", but told fans he will "look forward to seeing you all soon".

Kiwanuka simultaneously announced the release of his fifth album, titled Fudge, which was recorded before the stroke.

"I'm very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge," his message said.

"I'm especially happy because the last few months I've been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future. A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure.

"It's a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon.

"I'm not sure when I'll be able to be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done, it's a long, tough journey ahead but I'm fighting to get better.

"It has been a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now."

He thanked "all the incredible NHS staff and every single medical professional who has helped care for me and continue to help and encourage me in my recovery", and his friends and family for their support.

"This has definitely been one of the toughest challenges I've faced and I'll be happy to be on the other side of it when the time comes. Until then I wish you all well and look forward to seeing you further down the road."

Fans and fellow artists sent well wishes, with BBC Radio 6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne replying: "So sorry to read this, Michael. What a time you must have had. Really glad you have good care and wishing you a full recovery asap. One day at a time. Xx."

US singer Miguel wrote: "Man, take your time healing, you are needed brother."

Radiohead guitarist Ed O'Brien posted: "Sending love to you Michael."

Kiwanuka first made his mark 15 years ago, being named the BBC's Sound of 2012 , and has established himself as one of Britain's most acclaimed singers and songwriters.

His first three albums were nominated for the prestigious Mercury Prize for best British or Irish album of the year. He won the trophy in 2020 with his third record, Kiwanuka.

That album also earned him nominations for best male solo artist and album of the year at the Brits, and best rock album at the Grammy Awards.

He is also known for the song Cold Little Heart, which was used as the theme tune for US TV drama Big Little Lies.

But in July 2025 he cancelled all live shows on medical advice because of what was described as "continued illness".

articles.title: Trump-Xi summit should make sure American strength delivers American results
articles.summary: President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington with leverage on critical minerals, semiconductors and sanctions against Russia and Iran.
articles.body: It may not command the loudest headlines, but beneath the noise of the 24-hour news cycle, one of the most consequential foreign policy meetings of our time is taking shape as President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare to meet in Washington, D.C. There is no shortage of crises competing for our world’s attention. Ukraine continues to withstand Russia’s war of aggression, conflicts persist in the Middle East, illicit fentanyl devastates our communities, and the costs of essential goods remain far too high. At first glance, these challenges may seem far removed from one another, and certainly farther from a summit in Washington. They are not. CHINA’S XI SET TO ARRIVE IN WASHINGTON FOR HIGH-STAKES TRUMP SUMMIT AS AI SUPREMACY BATTLE LOOMS LARGE Underneath each of these pressures — quietly sustaining Russia and Iran, engineering fentanyl precursors, sowing disinformation and disrupting global supply chains — is a common thread: the Chinese Communist Party and its persistent pursuit of power to reshape the global order. China is a formidable adversary, but America is not coming to the table empty-handed. Congress and the administration have taken deliberate steps to reduce the vulnerabilities Beijing has exploited for decades. Through Project Vault, launched in February, we are building a domestic critical mineral stockpile so American manufacturers are not left at the mercy of foreign supply cuts. My bipartisan DOMINANCE Act, which passed the House in June, will help make America — not China — the partner of choice for nations developing their resources. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD Last week, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law, giving our government stronger tools to target entities bankrolling our adversaries, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s Operation Economic Fury is directly targeting the revenue streams sustaining the Iranian regime. This Congress has positioned America with leverage. Now is the time for Trump to translate that leverage into the results our nation and our world, need. Today, I am leading a bipartisan letter to the president outlining how he can do exactly that. IRAN TAPS FINANCIAL LIFELINE, RUSSIAN ARMS AS TRUMP ESCALATES 'CRUSHING' ECONOMIC WARFARE Start with our people. American citizens should never be used as bargaining chips, yet Beijing consistently and arbitrarily detains Americans on baseless charges. On June 3, Chinese authorities detained American scholar Min Zin after he was invited to attend an academic event. Dr. Youlin Chen, another American citizen, has spent more than 600 days behind bars without trial or access to his family. And while he is a British citizen, not American, Jimmy Lai remains behind bars in Hong Kong for simply running a free press. Trump knows that direct diplomacy can bring people home. When he personally raised the case of Pastor Ezra Jin with Xi, the pastor was released months later. Trump must look Xi in the eye and demand the immediate release of Min Zin, Youlin Chen, Jimmy Lai and every wrongfully detained American. TRUMP SHOULD PRESS XI ON CHINA’S PERSECUTION OF BELIEVERS AT HOME AND ABROAD We must also confront Beijing’s economic coercion head-on. China has spent decades tightening its grip on the critical minerals that power modern American life, from our smartphones and our automobiles to America’s most critical defense technologies. In June, Beijing yet again demonstrated its willingness to turn global critical mineral supply chains into shackles, placing American companies like MP Materials and USA Rare Earth on its export-control blacklist. While a short-term agreement for supply stabilization from this summit would be welcome, temporary relief cannot become permanent dependence. Then there is the elephant in the room. Beijing cannot claim to seek global stability while helping sustain the regimes that create chaos around the world. Chinese purchases of Russian and Iranian energy fuel Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war machine and Tehran and its destabilizing proxies. CHINA HAS A CHOKEHOLD ON YOUR MEDICINE CABINET. IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT Trump should make it unmistakably clear that any bank or entity helping our adversaries evade U.S. sanctions will face severe economic consequences. If Beijing wants access to the benefits of the global economy, it must abide by the rules. This Congress has positioned America with leverage. Now is the time for Trump to translate that leverage into the results our nation and our world, need. Today, I am leading a bipartisan letter to the president outlining how he can do exactly that. Finally, peace and stability must hold in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan produces more than 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors and is the United States’ fourth-largest trading partner. For our community here in Southern California, those stakes are too high to ignore. IRAN’S DEEPEST WEAKNESS IS GETTING EXPOSED THROUGH AMERICA’S MAXIMUM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN Our region is a gateway to the Pacific Rim, and businesses throughout my district rely directly on goods and commerce flowing safely through the Indo-Pacific. A blockade or military conflict would impact global markets and raise costs for Americans already stretching every dollar. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION That is why what happens in Washington this week matters more than the news cycle can tell. Foreign policy may be negotiated in diplomatic halls, but its consequences are felt at ports, factories, mom-and-pop shops and kitchen tables across our nation. If he uses it to secure clear, verifiable commitments, history will remember this summit not just for what was said across the table, but for what changed because of it. articles.title: 70,000-page chargesheet filed in Ayodhya Ram Temple donation case, SIT flags 105 instances of cash diversion
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: The Supreme Court-mandated Special Investigation Team (SIT) on Wednesday filed a nearly 70,000-page chargesheet against eight arrested accused in
articles.body: LUCKNOW: The Supreme Court-mandated Special Investigation Team (SIT) on Wednesday filed a nearly 70,000-page chargesheet against eight arrested accused in the Ram Temple donation embezzlement case before the additional district judge (Corruption) Court in Ayodhya.The chargesheet names Ram Shankar Yadav alias Tinnu, Anukalp Mishra, Avinash Shukla, Karunesh Pandey, Manish Yadav, Lavkush Mishra, Ramashankar Mishra and Subhash Srivastava.It was filed within the statutory 90-day period from the first arrest and includes charges of criminal breach of trust and offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act.The case was registered in June after the SIT's preliminary probe flagged suspected diversion of temple donations. Investigators recovered Rs 79.85 lakh in cash allegedly linked to the embezzlement from all accused except Srivastava.The document spans around 70,000 pages, including annexures, over 100 case diaries, statements of nearly 190 witnesses, banking records, property details, asset trails and findings of a forensic audit.The SIT was set up following the Supreme Court's orders on July 13. It is headed by Lucknow range inspector general of police Kiran S, along with DIG Faizabad Range Somen Barma and SSP, Ayodhya Gaurav Grover.The SIT uncovered 105 instances of unauthorised removal or concealment of cash during the counting process inside the temple premises.The probe tracked donations from collection boxes and counters to bank deposits. While investigators found evidence of cash being siphoned off during counting, they found no signs of pilferage during its transfer to banks.The SIT also verified 803 valuable donated articles recorded in the temple trust's software and found no discrepancies. Another 86 valuables without receipts were physically verified to check for any unaccounted donations.The investigators further examined donations of silver, including 200 kg of silver bricks, a 38.288-kg consignment, a silver necklace, Charan Paduka and a copy of the Ramcharitmanas.Around 944.411 kg of silver sent to the Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Ltd for melting was also verified.The SIT scrutinised bank accounts, deposits, withdrawals, properties, vehicles, jewellery and construction expenditure of the accused to trace the money trail and assess whether their assets were disproportionate to known sources of income.A forensic audit formed a key part of the investigation, officials said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news.
